title: AI Payment Agent Guardrails: How to Control Spending and Approvals
summary: Set AI payment controls for spending limits, delegated authorisation, consent and fraud checks. Learn how merchants can secure agent-led payment flows.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


A good AI agent is useful when it pays bills. However, an AI agent that can pay any amount without limits is a big problem. More payments will soon begin and end through AI assistants. Therefore, merchants need to determine who authorized each payment made using an AI assistant, how much the AI assistant was permitted to spend on behalf of the consumer, and ultimately who is liable in the event something goes wrong.


The purpose of this article is to explain the guardrails that control the use of[AI payment agents](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/what-is-agentic-commerce/) , the tools available for merchants to implement their own guardrails, and how the payment rail infrastructure in India is evolving.


### Key Takeaways


- AI payment agent guardrails define what an agent can buy, where it can pay, how much it can spend and when permission expires.
- Enforce limits in the payment or authorisation layer. Instructions in a prompt are not a reliable spending control.
- Delegated payment authorisation needs evidence of the customer’s permission and checks that each payment fits that permission.
- Approval, authentication, fraud screening, revocation and audit records work together. Their implementation depends on the payment flow.


##


Why Agentic Commerce Security Needs Additional Controls


Fraud and anti-money laundering (AML) systems have traditionally focused on monitoring individuals. These systems typically identify users based upon patterns and flag transactions outside of those patterns. Agents disrupt that paradigm. Agents can execute a transaction at any time and behave differently from human shoppers. Distinguishing an agent used maliciously from an agent used lawfully therefore requires more than recognising automation.


Another issue arises regarding authorization. While a customer may approve of a general rule for all payments executed by the agent, that rule does not by itself provide sufficient evidence that a specific transaction was within the approved scope. This is particularly important should a customer dispute a payment after it has been executed.


Consumers are aware of these issues. According to[Riskified’s Q1 2026 survey](https://www.riskified.com/press/riskified-agentic-commerce-pulse/) of 2,000 consumers across the U.S. and U.K., 73.9 percent of respondents expected safeguards such as biometric verification or a one-time passcode for agent transactions. This describes the surveyed consumers, rather than Indian regulatory requirements.


##


What Are AI Payment Agent Guardrails?


AI payment agent guardrails are limitations placed upon an agent in terms of utilizing a customer’s funds. The limitations serve to define four primary parameters:


- What types of goods or services can the agent utilize the customer’s funds to acquire?
- Within a single transaction, how much can the agent utilize the customer’s funds? Additionally, within a defined period of time (e.g. per day), how much can the agent utilize the customer’s funds?
- Where and during what time frames can the agent initiate payment(s)?
- What documentation serves to demonstrate that the customer has agreed to allow the agent to perform such actions?


Effective guardrails are established across multiple entities. Such entities include but are not limited to: the customer, the payment network, the payment provider and yourself, i.e. the merchant. Spending and permission checks should be enforced outside the language model, before a payment request is executed. A prompt telling an agent not to overspend is not a substitute for an enforced limit.


##


Delegated Payment Authorisation: How Does It Work?


A delegation of payment authority allows a client to delegate a third-party representative an authorization to make payments on their behalf up to certain limits without having to share their card number or UPI PIN.


One protocol that Google developed to support this type of functionality is called the[Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)](https://ap2-protocol.org/ap2/specification/) . Its current specification defines two main types of digitally signed mandates:


**Checkout mandate:** This mandate outlines the conditions under which the purchase will occur. Examples include price limitations, timing and product features. An open checkout mandate records constraints before the final purchase is selected.


A closed checkout mandate contains all products selected by the client, pricing, terms of sale, etc., for the current shopping cart. Earlier AP2 descriptions used intent and cart mandate terminology; use the version required by your integration.


**Payment mandate:** This mandate records the authorization to use a specific payment instrument for the checkout. It can also have open and closed forms.


These mandates create a digital record. In cases where a payment is determined to be fraudulent or incorrect, this record provides evidence of what was authorized. It does not automatically decide which party is legally responsible.


In addition to mandates,[tokens provide additional security](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/types-of-tokenization-integration/) . Card networks offer agentic tokens which represent the customers’ credit cards in supported agent-led transactions. Tokens can be limited to a specific merchant or use case, therefore a stolen token could do much less damage than a stolen credit card number. The available restrictions depend on the token program.


##


AI Agent Spending Limits: What UPI Supports


There are existing UPI tools that can support controlled spending in eligible flows. These are different from a universal permission for any AI agent to debit an account.


Reserve Pay works using a single block, multi-debit model. The consumer initially authorizes the amount to be reserved; eligible purchases at the merchant then make successive debits from these blocked funds until either the maximum allowable amount is depleted or the mandate expires. Any unused amounts are unblocked for the consumer when the mandate is canceled. This is not a separate reserve account.


UPI Circle illustrates how delegating spending limits functions. A primary consumer may designate up to 5 secondary consumers. In supported full-delegation flows, secondary consumers are permitted to make transactions of no greater than ₹5,000 per transaction and ₹15,000 monthly, subject to applicable conditions and any lower user limits. Primary consumers may approve each individual transaction or permit payments within a certain threshold and also revoke delegated access at any point.


NPCI also describes AI/software-driven IoT payments as a limited closed-user-group pilot. Its published device limits include ₹5,000 per transaction, ₹15,000 monthly and ₹2,000 during the first 24 hours after linking. These pilot permissions are not generally available to every agent. Our[agentic UPI guide](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/agentic-upi-payments-in-india/) explains the distinction between supported delegation and customer-approved QR checkout.


##


Indian Authentication Requirements for AI Agent Payments


India’s RBI issued updated authentication requirements as part of its[Authentication Mechanisms for Digital Payment Transactions Directions, 2025](https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/NotificationUser.aspx?Id=12898) , released on 25 September 2025. Compliance was required by 1 April 2026, unless otherwise specified.


In this regulatory environment, domestic digital payments must meet minimum requirements for authentication using at least two different forms of verification (i.e., two distinct factors), unless exempted. For digital payments other than card-present ones, at least one factor must be dynamically created or proven, with proof unique to that transaction. The e-mandate framework provides exemptions for eligible subsequent recurring transactions; other exemptions also apply. Therefore, customer authentication of payment flows and/or setting up mandates compliant with the current rules must be assessed for each agent transaction in India. An AI agent does not create a new exemption. Separate provisions cover specified cross-border card transactions.


##


Pre-Authorised Spending vs Per-Payment Approval


All agents require a different amount of supervision. There are some agent payments using scoped credentials and predetermined limits. Other flows ask the customer to accept the charge for each transaction.


An easy method to describe this situation: you can think of lower-value/repeat transactions (such as your weekly grocery order) in terms of the limits you have already established with the customer, provided the payment flow supports pre-authorisation. A higher/larger/unusual transaction may need to be accepted by the customer before it can be processed. The customer determines limits within the applicable payment rules. Your responsibility as a merchant is to adhere to the established limits, and to make the transition to step-up approval as seamless as possible when a transaction exceeds these limits. Fresh approval does not override network or regulatory restrictions.

##


AI Payment Controls Merchants Should Configure


The first step toward establishing merchant, network and customer guardrails is to understand the importance of implementing additional controls for merchant use cases. These are implementation controls to assess, rather than features automatically included in every payment product.


### 1. Set AI Agent Spending Limits


Set limits on agent purchase requests. Determine a maximum allowable value for agent initiated purchases and require a new authorization request for amounts over that limit.


### 2. Review Fraud Rules for Machine Buyers


Create machine buyer rules based upon device and behavior characteristics. Since the device and behavioral characteristics of legitimate agent activity can also trigger false positives for suspicious agent traffic, review your[fraud rules](https://www.cashfree.com/risk-shield-payment-gateway/) to ensure you detect malicious agent traffic while allowing legitimate agent traffic.


### 3. Verify Agent Identity and Authority


Identify legitimate vs. malicious bot agents. Identify the authorized agents permitted to perform transactions on your website and take a higher degree of skepticism towards unrecognized agents.


### 4. Keep Order and Payment References Connected


Label every agent transaction. Assign an identifier to every agent-placed order to enable your financial and customer service staff to track it throughout the process, including[settlement reconciliation](https://www.cashfree.com/settlement-and-reconciliation-guide/) , refunds and potential[chargeback processes](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/payment-disputes/) .


### 5. Record Customer Approval


Document approval. Record evidence of customer approval, when and for what amount(s). This can provide supporting evidence if there is a future dispute. Keep payment credentials, PINs and authentication secrets out of these logs.


### 6. Make Consent Visible and Revocable


Show consent to customers. Provide clear visibility to customers regarding what an agent is permitted to purchase or spend, and allow customers to revoke their consent at any time. Revocation should stop future use of that authority; it does not undo an already completed payment.


### An Example of Enforced AI Payment Controls


The following are illustrative business settings, not RBI or UPI limits. Apply whichever customer, product or network restriction is stricter.


**Control** **Example policy** **What the system should enforce**


Transaction limit Up to ₹2,000 per authorised purchase Block requests above the ceiling or obtain a new valid approval before payment


Cumulative budget Up to ₹5,000 within the approved period Account for pending and completed requests so parallel attempts cannot exceed the budget


Merchant and expiry Approved merchant IDs until the stated end time Reject other destinations and expired or revoked permissions


Retry protection One successful payment for each order Check payment status before retrying and prevent duplicate fulfilment


Use server-side policy checks before executing payment requests. Treat order creation, payment retries and[duplicate webhook handling](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/online/webhooks/webhook-indempotency) as separate checks; deduplicating notifications alone does not stop an agent from submitting a second payment request. Test these paths in a sandbox before live use.

##


Agentic Commerce Security Risks to Prepare For


There will always be a few agentic commerce security issues even if there are many guardrails in place.


**Hijacked agents** : Systems need to be able to determine when automation is being used by a legitimate entity versus an automated agent that has been compromised.


**Disagreements over unclear evidence** : If the consent to use the automation was granted via a very general mandate, then determining exactly what the shopper agreed to can be difficult.


**Uncertainty around liability** : In the Q1 2026 shopper study referenced above, 50.8% of customers believed the AI platform should be liable for unauthorized or erroneous purchases; 23.2% believed that the store/brand should be liable; and 18.7% believed they (the shopper) should be liable. These survey opinions do not determine which party would be held accountable under applicable law, payment rules and contracts.


**Chain reaction** : One malfunctioning action can cause a chain reaction throughout connected agents and systems. Establish processes to stop new requests, investigate erroneous actions and allow humans to intervene. A refund or reversal must follow the payment’s supported process; cancelling agent access does not reverse a settled payment.


##


How We Build Controls into Agentic Payment Flows


Our[Agentic Payments Suite](https://www.cashfree.com/agentic-payments/) supports payment experiences built around customer authority. The approval model depends on the product and supported flow.


**Cashfree Here:** Allows businesses to receive UPI and card payments within supported AI chats. Card information is entered into a sandboxed iframe and does not get passed to the AI model. Each transaction includes a recorded customer approval, and the AI model cannot independently initiate, alter or confirm a payment. Passkey-based biometric authentication is available for supported card payments.


**[Checkout for Agents](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/cashfree-hosted-checkout-is-now-agent-ready-with-webmcp/) :** Allows AI agents to assist with checkout on our supported Hosted Checkout redirect page utilizing WebMCP, while the required customer authorization remains in effect. If a payment requires an OTP, the shopper enters it. In the desktop UPI QR flow, the shopper scans and approves using their UPI PIN. Agents do not enter card details, CVV or OTPs.


**RiskShield:** Real-time fraud screening of payment transactions. Risk screening complements customer approval and spending permissions; it does not replace them.


**[Cashfree Wallet](https://www.cashfree.com/cashfree-wallet/) :** In its invite-only beta, customers can approve an agent task upfront with a budget, a number of payments and a consent duration. They receive payment alerts and can revoke access. The current offering supports bill payments; travel, food, groceries and shopping are listed as coming soon. This is a different approval model from our per-payment WebMCP QR flow.


Developers can explore payment flows in[Dev Studio](https://www.cashfree.com/devstudio) and validate the controls in their own integration. Product eligibility and supported permissions should be confirmed for the chosen flow.


##


Conclusion


A payment system using artificial intelligence cannot rely on AI alone for security. The ability to use artificial intelligence must have multiple controls to limit what it does and how much it spends. Those controls are:


- Customer limits
- Signed mandates or recorded customer approval, as applicable
- Restricted tokens
- Strong authentication
- Merchant rules that are specific to machine buyers.


If you implement these controls now, you can accept supported AI-led payments into your checkout process while maintaining control. Test the permitted, rejected and revoked-consent paths before expanding access.

##


FAQs


#### Does agentic payment security depend on one control or multiple controls?


Agentic payment security is a collection of controls that allow an artificial intelligence agent to only spend money when and where the customer wants them to within the amount they want to spend using recorded evidence that the customer gave permission for the spending.


##### Does delegated payment authorisation mean sharing a card number or UPI PIN?


Delegating payment authority allows the customer to grant permission to an artificial intelligence agent to make payments on their behalf with certain conditions such as amount spent and frequency of payments without sharing their credit card numbers or UPI PINs. Examples of how this can be done include through use of signed mandates in platforms like AP2.


#### Can I set AI agent spending limits?


Yes. There are several ways that customers can do this using supported mandates and UPI capabilities such as Reserve Pay; similarly, merchants can also put caps on the amount of an order they allow to be initiated by an agent.


#### Will a payment made via an AI agent still require an OTP in India?


The RBI generally requires at least two-factor authentication for domestic digital payments unless exempted. However, there are exceptions to this requirement, including eligible subsequent recurring e-mandate transactions. The customer must authenticate as required by the payment flow; this does not mean an OTP is mandatory in every case. A UPI PIN or supported biometric flow may be used instead.


#### What are AI payment agent guardrails?


Guardrails refer to the rules and checks that restrict how much an AI agent may purchase, how much it can expend, where and when it can pay, and what documentation shows that the customer approved the transaction.


#### Who is responsible if an AI agent processes a wrongful payment?


Responsibility depends on applicable law, payment rules, contracts and the circumstances. Frameworks such as AP2 provide a record of what was authorized. This can support investigation and dispute handling, but it does not determine liability on its own.
